title: Gabber local duality for prime-power torsion coefficients
statement: Let $\ell$ be a prime, $r\geq1$, and $\Lambda=\mathbf Z/\ell^r\mathbf Z$. Let $X$ be a Noetherian excellent scheme on which $\ell$ is invertible [def-exc-excellent-ring], equipped with a dimension function $\delta$. If $K$ is a pinned potential dualizing complex on $(X,\delta,\Lambda)$ [def-per-potential-dualizing-complex], then $K$ is bounded constructible [def-weil-pbc-constructible-complexes], the functor $D_K=R\mathcal Hom_\Lambda(-,K)$ [def-pur-derived-internal-hom] preserves $D^b_c(X_{\mathrm{et}},\Lambda)$, and the evaluation-transpose map $M\to D_KD_KM$ is an isomorphism for every $M$ in that category, naturally in $M$.

source.place: Expose XVII, Theorem 6.1.1, with coefficient integer ell^r; Definitions 1.4.1 and 2.1.1–2.1.2 for geometric-fibre pinnings

proof.text: Use the current pinned-potential definition: the pinnings are isomorphisms on the residue-field etale sites, and their geometric fibres commute with the normalized codimension-one transitions, using the signed twist identifications. Thus the hypothesis is a potential complex in the sense of ILO XVII 2.1.2, not just a collection of costalk isomorphisms. The given pinned potential complex $K$ belongs to $D^b_c(X_{\mathrm{et}},\Lambda)$, and even has finite Tor amplitude, by the existence-and-uniqueness theorem with its constructibility conclusion. This proves the first assertion for the actual given $K$, since the comparison in that theorem respects its pinnings.

First prove preservation for field coefficients $\Lambda=\mathbf F_\ell$, by noetherian induction for all excellent schemes and potential complexes. An ordinary constructible sheaf $M$ is lisse on a dense open $j:U\hookrightarrow X$: choose lisse neighborhoods of the finitely many generic points in a constructible stratification and remove their closed complements. Let $i:Z\hookrightarrow X$ be the reduced closed complement. Both $U$ and $Z$ remain excellent, by excellence of finite-type algebras and localizations. In the open--closed triangle $j_!j^*M\to M\to i_*i^*M$, the internal-adjunction formulas identify the duals of the two outside terms with $Rj_*R\mathcal Hom(j^*M,j^*K)$ and $i_*R\mathcal Hom(i^*M,i^!K)$. Open restriction $j^*K$ is potential for $\delta|_U$ by regular pullback pinnings: an open immersion is flat with fibres that are single reduced points or empty, hence regular, and its fibre local rings have dimension zero. Closed exceptional restriction $i^!K$ is potential by exceptional pullback: $i$ is proper, with compactification $(\mathrm{id}_Z,i)$. The latter dual is bounded constructible on $Z$ by the induction hypothesis. For the former, etale locally $j^*M$ is finite free over $\mathbf F_\ell$ in degree zero, so it is site-perfect, and the Ext-sheaf constructibility lemma (with $E=\mathbf Q_\ell$, $n=1$, so $A=\mathbf F_\ell$) makes every cohomology sheaf of $R\mathcal Hom(j^*M,j^*K)$ constructible on $U$. Internal Hom commutes with slice restriction, so on each member of an etale trivializing cover this complex is a finite direct sum of restrictions of $j^*K$; finitely many members suffice since $U$ is quasi-compact, so its cohomology lies in the bounded interval of $j^*K$ and it is bounded constructible on $U$. Direct-image finiteness applies to $j$ and $i$ since they are finitely presented over the excellent Noetherian target, so both outside duals are bounded constructible on $X$.

source.place: XVII, proof of Proposition 6.2.3.1: locally constant sheaves and noetherian devissage

proof.text: Apply the contravariant triangulated functor $D_X$ to the open--closed triangle of step 2. Its two outside duals are bounded constructible, so triangulated closure of $D^b_c$ gives the same for $D_XM$. For nonempty $X$ the chosen dense open is nonempty, so its closed complement is proper; the empty scheme starts the noetherian induction. This proves preservation for ordinary constructible $\mathbf F_\ell$-sheaves. Finally the ordinary truncation triangles build any bounded complex from its finitely many shifted cohomology sheaves; applying $D_X$ and triangulated closure proves preservation for all $D^b_c$ complexes over $\mathbf F_\ell$.

For $\Lambda=\mathbf Z/\ell^r\mathbf Z$, set $K_1=R\mathcal Hom_\Lambda(\mathbf F_\ell,K)$. The coefficient-restriction lemma makes $K_1$ a pinned potential complex for $(X,\delta,\mathbf F_\ell)$. Filter an ordinary constructible $\Lambda$-sheaf $M$ by $M\supseteq\ell M\supseteq\cdots\supseteq\ell^rM=0$. Each quotient $Q_a=\ell^aM/\ell^{a+1}M$ is constructible over $\mathbf F_\ell$. The coinduction comparison identifies $D_KQ_a$ with $D_{K_1}Q_a$, which is bounded constructible by steps 2–3. Forgetting the field action keeps the same finite stalks and cohomological bounds. Apply the exactness of $D_K$ to the finite filtration triangles, then to the ordinary truncation triangles of any bounded constructible complex. This proves preservation of $D^b_c(X_{\mathrm{et}},\Lambda)$ for every $r$.

source.place: XVII, Proposition 6.2.1.1 and proof of Proposition 6.2.3.1

proof.text: Write $\eta_M:M\to D_K^2M$ for the natural evaluation-transpose map, and work first with ordinary constructible sheaves. Weak biduality says that $\eta_M$ is an isomorphism in all degrees at most zero. Thus it remains to prove $\mathcal H^q(D_K^2M)=0$ for $q\geq1$. For a regular $p:Y\to X$, use the current fibrewise pinning theorem for ordinary pullback: it makes $p^*K$ potential for $\delta_Y(y)=\delta_X(p(y))-\dim\mathcal O_{Y_{p(y)},y}$, with geometrically regular fibres tested after finite residue-field extensions. At $y$, its fibrewise construction first localizes the base at $p(y)$, applies the supported base-change comparison on that localized scheme, and then applies the inverse point Gysin class in $\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O_{Y_{p(y)},y}$. The theorem states that these pinnings respect specialization, open restriction and composition. Internal-Hom base change gives $p^*D_KM\cong D_{p^*K}p^*M$. By step 4 the first dual is bounded constructible, so a second application gives $p^*D_K^2M\cong D_{p^*K}^2p^*M$, identifying the two evaluation maps. In particular the assertion can be tested after every strict localization, whose source is excellent Noetherian and has finite Krull dimension.

source.place: XVII, Propositions 4.1.1, 4.2.2, Lemma 4.3.1.1, Propositions 6.2.3.2 and 6.3.1; beginning of 6.5

proof.text: Prove biduality for all schemes of finite Krull dimension by induction on the dimension bound $d\geq0$. For dimension less than zero only the empty scheme occurs, and its only module complex is zero, with invertible evaluation. For fixed $d$, assume biduality for every constructible sheaf on every excellent scheme of dimension less than $d$ with the given coefficient ring and any dimension function. Within this induction, prove for $q=1,2,\ldots$ that $\mathcal H^q(D^2M)=0$ for all constructible sheaves on all such schemes of dimension at most $d$; at the $q$th stage assume this for all positive degrees less than $q$. These are simultaneous hypotheses for all schemes and sheaves, not hypotheses on only the current $X$ or $M$.

source.place: XVII, 6.5, the dimension induction and Definition 6.5.1

proof.text: At this induction stage the vanishing condition in degree $q$ is closed under subobjects and extensions. Indeed, a short exact sequence $0\to M\prime\to M\to M\prime\prime\to0$ gives a double-dual triangle. For $q>1$, its long exact sequence begins at this spot as $0\to\mathcal H^qD^2M\prime\to\mathcal H^qD^2M\to\mathcal H^qD^2M\prime\prime$, since the degree $q-1$ term vanishes by the inner induction. For $q=1$, weak biduality identifies the preceding map with the surjection $M\to M\prime\prime$, again giving the initial zero. Hence zero in the middle forces zero on the subobject, and zero on both outer terms forces zero in the middle.

Apply the normal-complete reduction with these dimension and degree induction hypotheses, the preservation proved in step 4, and weak biduality. It suffices, when $d\geq2$, to prove $\mathcal H^q(D_X^2\Lambda_X)=0$ on each normal complete strictly henselian local $X$ of dimension $d$. When $d=0$ or $d=1$, that reduction has no remaining constant-sheaf hypothesis: the normal local models are regular and their normalized potential complexes are twist-shifts of the unit. Thus these two dimension base cases are included. Fix a remaining $X$ with $d\geq2$.

source.place: XVII, Lemma 6.5.5 and following reduction to the complete normal case

proof.text: Partial algebraization gives a finite surjection $p:X\prime\to X$, with $X\prime$ normal, a complete regular excellent local base $S$ of dimension $d-1$, a finite-type $Z\to S$, and $X\prime\cong\widehat{Z_{(\bar z)}}$, with regular completion map $c:X\prime\to Z_{(\bar z)}$. The outer induction gives biduality on every excellent scheme of dimension at most $d-1$. The local scheme $S$ is connected, regular and excellent, so the regular-unit lemma makes $-\dim\mathcal O_{S,s}$ a dimension function on $S$, and the finite-type dimension-function lemma (excellent schemes are universally catenary) gives one on $Z$. Finite-type propagation, applied with bound $d-1$, therefore gives biduality for the constant sheaf on $Z_{(\bar z)}$, for every dimension function and pinned potential complex there. Choose one and pull it back by $c$; the regular pullback pinnings make it a pinned potential complex on $X\prime$ for the induced dimension function. The regular base-change comparison, applied twice as in step 5, shows that $\Lambda_{X\prime}$ is reflexive for this potential complex. The normalization-independence assertion in the normal-complete reduction applies on $X\prime$: any two dimension functions on this connected scheme differ by a constant, and the corresponding twist-shift cancels in $D^2$. Thus this reflexivity also holds for the pinned potential complex $p^!K_X$. Thus $\mathcal H^q(D_{X\prime}^2\Lambda_{X\prime})=0$ for the finite-pullback normalization.

source.place: XVII, final paragraph of 6.5: partial algebraization and finite-type propagation

proof.text: For the finite map $p$, use the comparison with $K_{X\prime}=p^!K_X$. It identifies $\mathcal H^q(D_X^2p_*\Lambda_{X\prime})$ with $p_*\mathcal H^q(D_{X\prime}^2\Lambda_{X\prime})=0$. Because $p$ is surjective, the unit $\Lambda_X\hookrightarrow p_*\Lambda_{X\prime}$ is a monomorphism of constructible sheaves. The subobject closure established in step 7 gives $\mathcal H^q(D_X^2\Lambda_X)=0$. This supplies the constant-sheaf hypothesis of step 8, which then gives degree-$q$ vanishing for every constructible sheaf on every scheme of dimension at most $d$.

source.place: XVII, Lemma 6.5.3 and final sentences of 6.5

proof.text: Induction on $q$ gives all positive-degree vanishings. Weak biduality then makes $\eta_M$ an isomorphism for every ordinary constructible sheaf in dimensions at most $d$, completing the outer induction. For an arbitrary $X$ of the statement, with no global finite-dimensional assumption, pull back to each strict localization; step 5 and the finite-dimensional result show that every pullback of $\eta_M$ is an isomorphism. Strict-local testing therefore gives biduality on $X$. Finally, use the finite truncation filtration of a bounded constructible complex and the morphism-of-triangles property of $\eta$ to pass from ordinary constructible sheaves and their shifts to every $M\in D^b_c$. The transformation is natural by its evaluation construction, so this proves the asserted natural biduality isomorphisms.

proof_origin.place: Expose XVII, 6.2–6.5, proof of Theorem 6.1.1, using Expose V 3.1.3–3.1.4

Internal Hom commutes with etale slice restriction; used to compute the dual of a finite locally constant field sheaf.
Closed immersions are proper, so their exceptional restrictions have the compactification required by the potential-pullback theorem.
